laws.title: Absolute Zero Tolerance for Drink Driving
laws.subtitle: Zákon č. 361/2000 Sb. — 0.0g/L BAC
laws.fullDescription: Czech Republic has absolute zero tolerance — any detectable alcohol while driving is illegal. Very strict enforcement.
laws.penalty: Any detectable alcohol: fine up to CZK 50,000, 1-year ban. Aggravated: imprisonment up to 3 years.
exceptions: None — zero tolerance with no exceptions
laws.sourceLabel: Zákon č. 361/2000 Sb. — Czech Traffic Law

quiz.q: Czech Republic's BAC limit for drivers?
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic has absolute zero tolerance — any detectable alcohol is illegal.

laws.title: Czech Culture — Beer Heritage and Reserved Warmth
laws.subtitle: World's highest beer consumption; formal until warmed up
laws.fullDescription: Czechs have the world's highest beer consumption per capita — beer culture is central to social life. Initially reserved with strangers; warm with friends. Formal address (pan/paní) with strangers. When toasting beer (Na zdraví!), make eye contact with everyone. Punctuality expected. Prague is cosmopolitan; rural areas are more traditional.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — pushiness or excessive informality before trust is built is unwelcome.
exceptions: Prague is much more internationally oriented
Younger generations are more casual

quiz.q: What must you do when toasting in Czech Republic?
options: Make eye contact with everyone you clink glasses with
quiz.explanation: When saying 'Na zdraví' (cheers) in Czech Republic, you must make direct eye contact with each person you clink glasses with.

laws.title: Drug Laws — Zero Tolerance; Cannabis Technically Illegal
laws.subtitle: Zákon o návykových látkách — Small amounts: fine + treatment
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic decriminalised possession of small amounts of drugs in 2010 — cannabis up to 10g is an administrative offence (fine), as are small personal amounts of other drugs. However, all drugs remain illegal and dealing is a serious criminal offence. Contrary to popular belief (and Prague's party reputation), openly smoking cannabis in public can result in a police fine. Medical cannabis is legal since 2013.
laws.penalty: Up to 10g cannabis: administrative fine (CZK 15,000). Over 10g: criminal. Drug dealing: up to 18 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Medical cannabis with prescription (since 2013)
Personal amounts of hard drugs: administrative fine rather than criminal
laws.sourceLabel: Czech Narcotic Substance Act (Zákon č. 167/1998 Sb.)

quiz.q: What quantity of cannabis triggers only an administrative fine (not criminal) in Czech Republic?
quiz.explanation: Czech law decriminalised possession of up to 10 grams of cannabis in 2010 — making it an administrative offence (fine) rather than a criminal one.

laws.title: Prague Tourist Regulations — E-scooter and Bike Rules
laws.subtitle: Prague Municipal Ordinances — Zone restrictions for micromobility
laws.fullDescription: Prague has introduced strict regulations for rental e-scooters after overcrowding in the historic centre. E-scooters cannot be ridden or parked in designated 'no-go zones' in the Prague 1 historic district (UNESCO World Heritage site). Only licensed operators with city permission can operate fleets. Cycling on pavements in the city centre is also prohibited. Segways are banned on pedestrianised areas.
laws.penalty: Riding e-scooter in no-go zone: fine CZK 2,500. Pavement cycling in historic centre: fine. Parking e-scooter in prohibited zone: removal + operator fine.
exceptions: Designated cycling lanes throughout the city
Outside the historic centre zone, rules are less strict
laws.sourceLabel: Prague City Hall — E-scooter and Micromobility Ordinance

quiz.q: Where are e-scooters banned in Prague?
options: The Prague 1 historic district centre (UNESCO zone)
quiz.explanation: Prague banned e-scooters and restricted their parking in the Prague 1 historic district — a UNESCO World Heritage site — to protect the character of the historic centre.

laws.title: Prague Graffiti Laws — Heavy Fines for Historic Districts
laws.subtitle: Heritage Protection Act — Defacing buildings: criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Prague's Old Town (UNESCO World Heritage Site) is heavily protected from graffiti and vandalism. The Czech Heritage Protection Act makes defacing protected historic structures a criminal offence. Prague has been battling chronic graffiti problems — especially on historic building facades, Charles Bridge, and Prague Castle walls. Graffiti artists have been arrested and imprisoned. The city runs extensive restoration programmes. Taggers caught face criminal prosecution, restoration cost liability, and possible prison time.
laws.penalty: Graffiti on protected heritage structure: up to 3 years imprisonment + full restoration costs. Non-protected building: fine + restoration.
exceptions: Authorised street art zones in certain districts
Legal graffiti walls in Žižkov neighbourhood

quiz.q: What makes graffiti on Prague's historic buildings particularly serious legally?
options: Because they are UNESCO World Heritage structures — defacing them is a criminal offence carrying up to 3 years
Because spray paint is banned in Prague
Only the Charles Bridge is protected
quiz.explanation: Prague's Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — defacing its historic structures is a criminal offence under Czech heritage law, carrying up to 3 years imprisonment plus restoration costs.

laws.title: Czech Beer Culture Laws — Public Drinking and Municipal Rules
laws.subtitle: Municipal ordinances — public alcohol rules vary; cheapest beer in EU
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has the world's highest beer consumption per capita and beer is deeply embedded in national culture — a half-litre of beer in Prague often costs less than a bottle of water, making the Czech Republic home to some of the EU's cheapest pub beer. Unlike some European countries, public drinking is not banned at the national level, but many municipalities — including Prague — have introduced local ordinances restricting alcohol consumption in specific public spaces such as certain squares and playgrounds. Prague's City Hall created 'alcohol-free zones' in Wenceslas Square and near major tourist sites after disorder problems. Visitors should check local signage; fines are increasingly enforced by city wardens.
laws.penalty: Drinking in a designated alcohol-free municipal zone: on-the-spot fine CZK 1,000–10,000 (approx. €40–€400). Selling alcohol to minors under 18: criminal offence.
exceptions: Licensed outdoor terraces and beer gardens are fully permitted anywhere
Areas without municipal alcohol-free zone signage remain unrestricted
laws.sourceLabel: Prague City Hall — Alcohol-Free Zone Ordinances

quiz.q: Which country has the world's highest beer consumption per capita?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic holds the world record for beer consumption per capita — beer is central to Czech culture and often costs less than bottled water, reflecting centuries of brewing tradition including the birthplace of Pilsner lager in Plzeň.

laws.title: Prague Heritage Protection — Defacing Historic Buildings is a Criminal Offence
laws.subtitle: Zákon č. 20/1987 Sb. — UNESCO Old Town: graffiti = serious crime
laws.fullDescription: Prague's historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Czech Heritage Protection Act (Zákon č. 20/1987 Sb.) makes it a criminal offence to damage, deface, or alter any listed heritage structure without permission. Graffiti on historic buildings is prosecuted as vandalism with damage to cultural property — which carries significantly harsher penalties than ordinary graffiti. Prague has over 40,000 listed heritage structures. In 2019, Prague began prosecuting 'touristy vandalism' including lock bridges — the city has removed thousands of padlocks from bridges and imposed fines. Engraving names in stone is also prosecuted.
laws.penalty: Damage to listed cultural monument: up to 2 years imprisonment + restitution costs. Graffiti on UNESCO heritage buildings: criminal charges + full restoration costs (often €5,000–50,000).
exceptions: Authorised restoration work by licensed conservators
Approved street art commissions in non-heritage areas

quiz.q: Approximately how many listed heritage structures does Prague have?
quiz.explanation: Prague has over 40,000 listed heritage structures — one of the densest concentrations of protected buildings in Europe, making it an exceptionally sensitive environment for vandalism.

laws.title: Dog Laws — Muzzle Requirements and Strict Leash Rules in Czech Cities
laws.subtitle: Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb. — Certain breeds muzzled; dog tax required in cities
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has specific rules for dogs in public. In Prague and most Czech cities, dogs must be on a leash in all public spaces including parks and pavements — leash-free areas (volno-běžecké zóny) are specifically designated. Certain breeds classified as 'dangerous' under Czech law (American Staffordshire Terrier, Staffordshire Bull Terrier, Rottweiler, Bull Terrier and their crosses) must be muzzled in all public spaces. Dog owners must register their pet and pay the local 'poplatek ze psa' (dog tax) — typically CZK 200–1,500 per year depending on the municipality. Leaving dog waste on public pavements is a fineable offence. Visiting tourists with dogs must carry proof of vaccination and an EU pet passport.
laws.penalty: Dog not on leash in restricted area: CZK 10,000–100,000 fine. Unregistered dog: administrative fine. Failing to clean up dog waste: CZK 1,000 fine.
exceptions: Designated off-leash dog parks (volno-běžecké zóny)
Police, military, and service dogs on duty
laws.sourceLabel: Czech Interior Ministry — Animal Control Regulations

quiz.q: What Czech tax must dog owners in cities pay annually?
quiz.explanation: Czech municipalities require dog owners to pay a 'poplatek ze psa' (dog tax) — typically CZK 200–1,500 per year depending on the city. Failing to register and pay can result in administrative fines.

laws.title: Czech Beer Culture — Protected Designations and Brewing Laws
laws.subtitle: Czech beer styles have EU Protected Geographical Indication status
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has the world's highest per-capita beer consumption and a 1,000-year brewing tradition codified in law. Czech beer styles including 'Česky ležák' (Czech lager) carry EU Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status — only beer brewed in the Czech Republic using traditional methods can use these designations. The 1997 Brewing Act regulates alcohol content labeling (Czech degrees Plato must be declared). Unpasteurized 'tank beer' (tankové pivo) served from pressurized tanks must meet strict freshness standards. Craft breweries must register with the Czech Customs Administration and pay excise tax. Traditional Czech brewing techniques are protected under heritage law.
laws.penalty: False PGI labeling: fines up to 50 million CZK (~$2.2M USD). Brewing without registration: fines up to 5 million CZK + shutdown.
exceptions: Home brewing up to 200 liters per household per year for personal consumption
Beer tourism demonstrations using traditional methods
EU-compliant imports with proper labeling
laws.sourceLabel: EU — Czech Beer Protected Geographical Indications

quiz.q: What is the world ranking of Czech Republic for per-capita beer consumption?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic consistently ranks first globally in per-capita beer consumption, with an average of around 140 liters per person per year — a figure tied to their centuries of brewing heritage.

laws.title: Velvet Revolution Legacy — November 17 National Day and Anti-Totalitarian Laws
laws.subtitle: Czech law commemorates 1989 revolution; collaboration with communist secret police (StB) is documented
laws.fullDescription: November 17 is both International Students Day (commemorating 1939 Nazi crackdown on Czech students) and the Czech Day of the Struggle for Freedom and Democracy (commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution start). Czech law (Act 198/1993) declared the communist regime (1948–1989) criminal, illegitimate, and condemnable — similar in spirit to Germany's Nazi prohibition laws. The Office for the Documentation and Investigation of Communist Crimes (ÚDV) investigates crimes from the communist era. The Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes (ÚSTR) and the Security Services Archive (ABS) opened StB (secret police) files, revealing informers — including public figures who had been secret collaborators. Being revealed as an StB collaborator carries severe social and political consequences though no criminal penalty in most cases.
laws.penalty: Communist-era crimes (murder, torture) not time-barred under 1993 Act: prosecuted as murder/assault. False denial of documented StB collaboration by public officials: potential defamation counter-claims.
exceptions: Statute of limitations has passed for most communist-era property crimes
Individuals who cooperated under coercion have different legal status than willing collaborators
Historical research and journalism using ABS archives is encouraged and protected
laws.sourceLabel: Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes — Czech Republic

quiz.q: What did Czech Act 198/1993 declare about the communist regime that governed from 1948-1989?
options: It declared amnesty for all crimes committed during the communist period
It declared the communist regime criminal, illegitimate, and condemnable
It established a reparations fund for communist-era victims
It banned former communist party members from public office
quiz.explanation: Czech Act 198/1993 (On the Illegality of the Communist Regime and on Resistance to It) declared the communist regime that governed Czechoslovakia from 1948–1989 to be criminal, illegitimate, and morally condemnable — providing a legal basis for prosecuting crimes committed in its service and opening its secret police archives.

laws.title: Bohemian Switzerland National Park — Czech-German Transboundary Protected Area
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic and Germany manage a shared national park; 2022 wildfire tested cross-border coordination
laws.fullDescription: Bohemian Switzerland National Park (established 2000) shares a boundary with Germany's Saxon Switzerland National Park — forming Europe's first transboundary national park. The parks protect Europe's northernmost sandstone rock formations, including the famous Pravčická brána (Bastei arch — Europe's largest natural sandstone arch). Czech Nature Conservation Law requires management plans jointly developed with German Sächsische Schweiz. In July–August 2022, a major wildfire burned 1,000+ hectares in Bohemian Switzerland — the Czech Republic's worst in modern history. Czech firefighters, German assistance, and helicopter support from multiple EU countries coordinated under EU Civil Protection Mechanism. The fire revealed gaps in Czech fire prevention law — regulations for prescribed burns in national parks were subsequently updated.
laws.penalty: Starting unauthorized fires in national park: criminal arson charges + civil liability for firefighting costs (potentially millions of CZK). Unauthorized camping (which risks fire): fines up to CZK 15,000. Vehicle access to restricted roads: fines.
exceptions: Park rangers conducting prescribed burns with park directorate authorization
Research stations monitoring fire ecology
Czech Army helicopter support operations during declared emergencies

quiz.q: What made Bohemian Switzerland National Park historically significant when established in 2000?
options: It was the Czech Republic's first national park
It was Europe's first transboundary national park, shared with Germany's Saxon Switzerland
It contained Europe's largest contiguous forest protected area
It was the first EU national park established under the Habitats Directive
quiz.explanation: When established in 2000, Bohemian Switzerland National Park and Germany's adjacent Saxon Switzerland National Park formed Europe's first transboundary national park — a jointly managed protected area crossing an international border. The parks share management protocols, visitor infrastructure, and emergency response plans.

laws.title: Velvet Divorce & Czech EU Presidency
laws.subtitle: Czechoslovakia's peaceful 1993 split remains a global model for negotiated national separation
laws.fullDescription: On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully dissolved into the Czech Republic and Slovakia — the 'Velvet Divorce' — becoming one of history's rare examples of negotiated national separation without violence. The split was driven by Slovak demands for greater autonomy and Czech reluctance to subsidize Slovakia's slower economic development. Importantly, no referendum was held; the separation was negotiated between political leaders. The Czech Republic went on to join NATO (1999) and the EU (2004). In 2022–2023, the Czech Republic held the EU Council Presidency during the critical period of coordinating European response to Russia's Ukraine invasion.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties — the Velvet Divorce was achieved through legislative action in both parliaments. Property and debt were divided proportionally (2:1 Czech to Slovak ratio based on population).
exceptions: Citizens of both countries received dual citizenship options for a transition period
Cultural institutions like shared museums divided collections through negotiation
Monetary union continued briefly before Czech and Slovak korunas separated in February 1993

quiz.q: What made the 1993 Czechoslovakia dissolution historically remarkable compared to most national separations?
options: It was approved by a 90% referendum vote
It was achieved peacefully through parliamentary legislation without violence or a referendum
It was mandated by the UN Security Council
It occurred after a civil war ceasefire
quiz.explanation: Czechoslovakia's 'Velvet Divorce' on January 1, 1993 is remarkable because it was achieved entirely peacefully through parliamentary legislation — no referendum, no violence — making it a rare global model for negotiated national separation.

laws.title: Energy Independence & Nuclear Expansion
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic accelerated nuclear power expansion to end dependence on Russian gas
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic was heavily dependent on Russian natural gas before the Ukraine war — over 95% of gas imports came from Russia via the Druzhba pipeline. Following the 2022 invasion, the Czech Republic rapidly diversified: LNG contracts with the US and Qatar, reverse gas flows from Germany, and a landmark 2024 contract with EDF (France) for up to four new nuclear reactors at Dukovany and Temelin — worth up to €400 billion over the plants' lifetime. The Czech Republic already operates 2 nuclear plants providing ~40% of electricity. PM Fiala made nuclear expansion a national priority, making Czech Republic Europe's most nuclear-ambitious country outside France.
laws.penalty: Tampering with nuclear facilities: up to 20 years imprisonment. Violations of SÚJB (State Office for Nuclear Safety) regulations: license revocation. Unauthorized uranium mining: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Czech nuclear waste is stored in intermediate storage with final repository site selection ongoing
Temelin and Dukovany plants are operated by ČEZ (state-majority utility)
EU state aid rules apply to nuclear contracts requiring European Commission approval
laws.sourceLabel: Czech State Office for Nuclear Safety

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Czech electricity was already provided by nuclear power before the new expansion?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic's existing nuclear plants at Dukovany and Temelin already provide approximately 40% of the country's electricity — and its landmark 2024 contract with EDF for up to four new reactors will make it even more nuclear-reliant than it already is.

laws.title: Velvet Revolution Day & Communist-Era Lustration Laws
laws.subtitle: Czechia celebrates the 1989 democratic revolution on November 17 and barred communist secret police collaborators from public office
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic celebrates November 17 as a national holiday — the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that peacefully ended Communist Party rule. Czechia's 'lustration' laws (Law 451/1991) were among the most comprehensive in post-communist Europe: they barred former Communist Party officials, StB secret police members and informants, and National Security Corps members from holding senior state positions for a transitional period. The Constitutional Court upheld the law. Jan Palach, who set himself on fire in 1969 to protest the Soviet invasion, is honored on January 16 (Palach Day) in Prague. Czechia's approach to transitional justice remains a model studied internationally.
laws.penalty: Knowingly falsifying a lustration certificate: criminal offense. Former StB informants discovered in senior positions: removal from office
exceptions: Lustration certificates were required for senior state, judicial, and academic positions
The time limits on some lustration provisions have gradually expired
laws.sourceLabel: Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes – Czech Republic

quiz.q: What did Czech 'lustration' laws (1991) prohibit communist-era secret police collaborators from doing?
quiz.explanation: Czech lustration laws barred former Communist Party officials and StB secret police collaborators from holding senior government, judicial, and academic positions — one of the most comprehensive transitional justice measures in post-communist Europe.

laws.title: Czech Artillery Initiative: Sourcing 800,000 Shells for Ukraine
laws.subtitle: The Czech Republic led a landmark international effort to procure ammunition for Ukraine outside EU frameworks when European production fell short
laws.fullDescription: In February 2024, Czech President Petr Pavel and PM Fiala announced that Czechia had identified 800,000 artillery shells available for purchase from non-EU countries for delivery to Ukraine — if EU partners would fund them. The 'Czech Initiative' became the most significant European ammunition effort of the war: by mid-2024, 18+ countries had contributed funds, and the first shells from outside Europe began arriving in Ukraine. The initiative exposed the EU's failure to meet its own ammunition production targets (1 million shells promised by March 2024 but only ~520,000 delivered). Czech law allows arms exports to conflict zones with government approval. Czechia is proportionally one of the largest per-GDP military aid donors to Ukraine.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized arms exports: up to 8 years imprisonment under Czech export control law. Licensed military exports to Ukraine are legal and encouraged
exceptions: EU coordination of military aid to Ukraine operates through the European Peace Facility — a separate funding mechanism
Czech domestic arms producers (ZB, CSG Group) have expanded production under government contracts

quiz.q: What was the Czech Republic's landmark contribution to Ukraine's ammunition crisis in 2024?
options: Identifying and coordinating international purchase of 800,000 artillery shells from non-EU sources
Donating its entire national artillery stockpile
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic identified 800,000 artillery shells available from non-EU sources and organized an international funding coalition to purchase them for Ukraine — filling a critical gap after the EU failed to meet its own 1-million-shell production promise.

laws.title: Beer Culture Protection
laws.subtitle: Czech law designates traditional pub culture as intangible cultural heritage
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic formally inscribed 'Czech Beer Culture' on its national list of Intangible Cultural Heritage (2023), recognizing the pivotal role of the pub (hospoda) in Czech social life. Beyond cultural recognition, Czech law regulates beer production through strict brewing standards: Czech lager must be brewed with Bohemian hops (Saaz hops from Žatec), Czech malt, and local water under the Czech Technical Standard ČSN. 'Czech beer' as a geographical indication is protected under EU law. The Czech Republic consistently leads the world in per-capita beer consumption.
laws.penalty: Misuse of 'Czech beer' geographic indication: fines under EU GI law; brewing standards violations: production licenses revoked
exceptions: Craft breweries can experiment with non-traditional recipes if not marketed as traditional Czech lager
Home brewing for personal consumption is legal

quiz.q: Which city is famous for producing the Saaz hops used in Czech lager?
quiz.explanation: Žatec (known in German as Saaz) is the historic hop-growing region of Bohemia, producing the aromatic hops that define Czech lager's distinctive flavor.

laws.title: Velvet Divorce Law
laws.subtitle: Czechoslovakia's peaceful split into two nations in 1993
laws.fullDescription: On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully dissolved into the Czech Republic and Slovakia — an event known as the 'Velvet Divorce,' echoing the 'Velvet Revolution' that ended communism in 1989. The Constitutional Act on the Dissolution of the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic (1992) was passed by the Federal Assembly with no public referendum. Division of assets, debts, the military, and embassies was handled through an extensive treaty framework. The dissolution was remarkably peaceful — no violence, no border conflicts, and the two countries immediately established close ties. Czech law inherited most Czechoslovak federal law and institutions.
laws.penalty: N/A — historical constitutional act; no individual penalties
exceptions: Dual citizenship rights were limited immediately after separation but have since been liberalized for those who held it
laws.sourceLabel: Chamber of Deputies of the Czech Republic

quiz.q: Was there a public referendum on the dissolution of Czechoslovakia?
options: No — it was decided by the Federal Assembly
Yes, but the vote was disputed
quiz.explanation: Despite polls showing most Czechs and Slovaks wanted the federation to continue, the Velvet Divorce was decided by politicians in the Federal Assembly without a public referendum — a decision that remains controversial to this day.

laws.title: Lustration Law
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic's lustration law barred former communist collaborators from public office
laws.fullDescription: Czechoslovakia's Lustration Act (1991, continued by the Czech Republic post-1993) prohibited former senior Communist Party officials, StB (secret police) members, and those who collaborated with the StB from holding high-ranking public offices, state enterprise positions, and security services roles for a period of five years (later extended multiple times). Czech lustration was one of the most comprehensive in post-communist Europe. The law required civil servants, judges, and senior officials to obtain a 'lustration certificate' from the Interior Ministry confirming they had no compromising communist-era records. It generated controversy over collective guilt and evidence quality.
laws.penalty: Occupying barred positions without a valid lustration certificate: criminal offense; false declarations: perjury charges
exceptions: Politicians elected to parliament were not subject to lustration — only appointed officials
Age-based exemptions applied to those who were too young during the communist era

quiz.q: What does 'lustration' mean in the context of post-communist transitions?
options: The process of rewriting history books
Screening public officials for collaboration with the former communist regime
quiz.explanation: Lustration (from Latin lustratio — purification) refers to the process of screening public officials for past collaboration with communist-era security services or party structures. Czech lustration was among Europe's most comprehensive screening programs.

laws.title: Constitutional Act on Dissolution of Czechoslovakia (1992)
laws.subtitle: The peaceful 'Velvet Divorce' split Czechoslovakia into two states without a referendum
laws.fullDescription: On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully dissolved into two independent states: the Czech Republic and Slovakia. This was achieved through Constitutional Act No. 542/1992 Coll. on the Dissolution of the Czech and Slovak Federal Republic, passed by the Federal Assembly in November 1992. Notably, the dissolution occurred without a referendum — polls showed most Czechs and Slovaks preferred to remain united, but the political leaders (Czech PM Václav Klaus and Slovak PM Vladimír Mečiar) agreed to separate. The 'Velvet Divorce' is studied as a model for peaceful state dissolution: property, international obligations, military assets, UN membership, and even the national debt were divided by negotiated formulas (generally 2:1 Czech to Slovak ratio reflecting population). Both states were recognized internationally within days. The Czech Republic assumed Czechoslovakia's UN seat and membership in international organizations.
laws.penalty: No penalties — this was a constitutionally-mandated state dissolution process; both successor states assumed equal international legal standing
exceptions: Citizens of the other state received dual-nationality transition periods
Properties straddling the new border required special negotiation
Cultural property (museums, archives) required separate bilateral agreements

laws.title: Lustration Law and Communist Era Accountability
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic's 1991 lustration law barred communist secret police collaborators from public office
laws.fullDescription: Czechoslovakia (and then the Czech Republic) enacted the Lustration Act (Act No. 451/1991) in October 1991 — one of the most comprehensive transitional justice laws addressing communist-era collaboration. The law barred former communist secret police (StB) officers and informants from holding senior positions in government, state enterprises, army, police, and academia for five years. The law required candidates for such positions to submit to a screening (lustration) process at the Ministry of Interior. Critics noted the process relied on StB records that were incomplete and sometimes contained errors or planted information; some individuals were falsely identified as informants. The Constitutional Court upheld the law's constitutionality. The lustration law was unique in Europe for its scope and was extended and modified multiple times. By contrast, Germany (de-Stasi) and Poland (lustracja) developed their own approaches. Czech President Havel supported lustration as necessary for democratic consolidation, though he expressed concerns about its limitations.
laws.penalty: Holding a screened position without proper lustration clearance: removal from office; false statements in lustration certificate applications: criminal prosecution
exceptions: The law had a 5-year limitation that was extended
Persons who collaborated under coercion had some procedural protections
Elected officials were not subject to lustration (constitutional distinction between elected and appointed positions)

laws.title: Czech Anti-Corruption Framework and Transparency Measures
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic strengthened asset disclosure and conflict of interest rules
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic under Prime Minister Petr Fiala (ODS coalition) has pursued anti-corruption and transparency reforms. The Conflict of Interest Act (Lex Babiš) was named after former PM Andrej Babiš, who was prosecuted for EU subsidy fraud related to his Stork Nest Farm. The Czech Supreme Court ultimately acquitted Babiš in 2023. The country strengthened the National Anti-Corruption Strategy 2022-2027, enhancing whistleblower protections and asset declaration requirements for public officials. Czech Republic has consistently ranked among Central Europe's least corrupt nations on Transparency International's index, though concerns about oligarchic media ownership persist.
laws.penalty: Public official asset declaration violations: fines up to CZK 500,000. Conflict of interest violations: fines up to CZK 1 million and disqualification.
exceptions: Small value gifts to officials (under CZK 300) permitted
Academic and journalistic activities not subject to conflict of interest restrictions

quiz.q: What was 'Lex Babiš' in Czech politics?
options: A law banning foreign ownership of Czech media
The Conflict of Interest Act named after former PM Andrej Babiš
An anti-immigration law supported by Babiš
A term limit law restricting third terms
quiz.explanation: Lex Babiš refers to Czech conflict of interest legislation (notably Act No. 159/2006) that was specifically relevant to Andrej Babiš's case, as it prohibits public officials from controlling media companies receiving public contracts.

laws.title: Czech Nuclear Expansion and Dukovany Power Plant
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic chose Westinghouse for a major new nuclear reactor amid energy independence drive
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic selected Westinghouse (US company) to build a new reactor at the Dukovany nuclear power plant in July 2024 — a major strategic decision that excluded Russian (Rosatom) and Chinese (CGN) bids for security reasons. The decision reflected Czech efforts to reduce energy dependence on Russia following the Ukraine war. Czech Republic gets approximately 40% of electricity from nuclear power and plans to expand this significantly. The government signed an intergovernmental agreement with the US to support the project. The Dukovany 5 reactor would be the first new Czech nuclear unit since the 1990s. Multiple additional reactors are also planned at Temelín.
laws.penalty: Nuclear safety violations: Criminal Energy Act and Atomic Act fines up to CZK 50 million. Unauthorized nuclear activity: criminal prosecution under Czech law.
exceptions: Existing Russian-designed reactors at Dukovany may continue operation under Czech State Office for Nuclear Safety oversight
Uranium sourcing diversified but Russian nuclear fuel still used in transition period
laws.sourceLabel: State Office for Nuclear Safety Czech Republic

quiz.q: Why did Czech Republic exclude Russian and Chinese bids for its Dukovany nuclear reactor?
options: Their cost bids were too high compared to Westinghouse
For security reasons — to avoid energy dependence on geopolitical rivals
Environmental regulations prohibited non-European reactor designs
EU state aid rules required a European bidder to win
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic excluded Rosatom (Russia) and CGN (China) on national security grounds — the Ukraine war had made Czech policymakers unwilling to create new energy dependencies on Russia, and China was excluded for similar strategic concerns.

laws.title: Czech Digital Services and AI Regulation
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic implements EU AI Act and DSA requirements
laws.fullDescription: As an EU member, the Czech Republic implements the EU AI Act and Digital Services Act (DSA). High-risk AI systems in healthcare, education, employment, and critical infrastructure require mandatory conformity assessments before deployment. The Czech Office for Personal Data Protection (ÚOOÚ) enforces GDPR and DSA. Very large online platforms must provide algorithmic transparency. Czech law additionally requires platforms to remove illegal content within 24 hours of a valid removal order.
laws.penalty: GDPR violations: up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. DSA non-compliance: up to 6% of global turnover. AI Act high-risk violations: up to €30 million or 6% of global turnover
exceptions: Small businesses under DSA thresholds have lighter obligations
Research and development AI use has specific exemptions
National security AI applications are outside EU AI Act scope
laws.sourceLabel: Czech Office for Personal Data Protection

quiz.q: Which Czech authority enforces GDPR and digital service regulations?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Office for Personal Data Protection (ÚOOÚ) is the national authority responsible for enforcing GDPR and digital services regulations in the Czech Republic.

laws.title: Czech Republic's Babis Trial and Corruption Cases
laws.subtitle: Former PM Babis acquitted of EU subsidy fraud amid controversy
laws.fullDescription: Former Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO party) was prosecuted for allegedly fraudulently obtaining EU subsidies by hiding ownership of the Stork Nest Farm to qualify as a small agricultural business. He was acquitted in 2023 after multiple trials. Despite the acquittal, the case raised significant conflict-of-interest questions — Babiš is a billionaire oligarch who controls major Czech media while serving as PM. The Czech Anti-Corruption Act (ROPO law) limits political officials from controlling media. EU anti-fraud office OLAF maintained fraud findings. Babiš ran again for president in 2023, losing narrowly.
laws.penalty: EU subsidy fraud: up to 10 years imprisonment. Abuse of public office: up to 10 years. Breach of conflict-of-interest rules: fines and removal from office. Babiš's case: acquitted — no penalty imposed. Czech presidents have prosecutorial immunity while in office
exceptions: Small agricultural subsidies under €10,000 have simplified oversight
EU audit rights extend to all subsidized entities regardless of political connections
Media ownership rules have grandfather provisions for existing owners

quiz.q: What EU body maintained fraud findings against Babiš despite his Czech court acquittal?
quiz.explanation: The EU's Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) maintained its fraud findings against Babiš despite his acquittal in Czech courts — illustrating how EU and national legal proceedings can reach different conclusions on the same facts.

laws.title: Czech Republic's OECD Tax and Digital Services Framework
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic implements global minimum corporate tax
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic, as an OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework member, implemented the Pillar Two global minimum corporate tax (15% minimum on large multinationals) through domestic legislation effective 2024. The Czech Top-up Tax Act ensures Czech-headquartered multinationals with global revenues over €750 million pay at least 15% effective tax rate. Czech Republic also signed up to the OECD's automatic exchange of financial account information (AEOI/CRS) with over 100 countries. The Czech tax authority also introduced broader e-reporting requirements for VAT and expanded electronic tax filing mandates.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with global minimum tax provisions: domestic top-up tax applied plus interest. Failure to file AEOI reports: fines up to CZK 500,000. VAT carousel fraud (common in Czech Republic): criminal prosecution, up to 10 years. Transfer pricing violations: back taxes plus 20% penalty
exceptions: Investment funds and pension funds have modified Pillar Two treatment
Substance-based income exemptions available for companies with genuine local operations
Small domestic companies are not subject to Pillar Two

quiz.q: What is the global minimum corporate tax rate that Czech Republic's 2024 Top-up Tax Act ensures large multinationals pay?
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic's 2024 Top-up Tax Act implements the OECD Pillar Two global minimum corporate tax of 15% for large multinationals — ensuring Czech-headquartered companies with €750m+ global revenues pay at least this rate regardless of where profits are booked.

laws.title: Czech Firearms Act and Expanded Gun Rights
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic has the most permissive gun laws in the EU
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has among the most liberal firearms laws in the European Union. The Arms and Ammunition Act allows Czech citizens to own firearms for self-defense, sport shooting, and collecting. Licensed citizens can carry concealed handguns after passing training and psychological tests. The Czech Republic pushed back against EU firearms directives that tried to restrict semi-automatic weapons, eventually receiving exemptions for competitive shooters. Gun ownership is considered a constitutional right in proposals that have passed Parliament. License holders must renew every 5 years with medical checks.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed firearm possession: up to 3 years imprisonment; trafficking in prohibited weapons: up to 8 years
exceptions: Licensed sport shooters can own otherwise restricted semi-automatic firearms
Antique firearms with historical exemptions

quiz.q: What makes Czech Republic firearms laws unusual in the EU?
options: They are among the most permissive, allowing licensed concealed carry
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic has among the most liberal firearms laws in the EU, allowing licensed citizens to own and carry firearms for self-defense after training, and has resisted EU directives seeking to tighten restrictions.

laws.title: Firearms Registration and Background Check Requirements
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic implemented stricter background checks while maintaining gun rights
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic aligned its firearms laws with EU Firearms Directive requirements while maintaining relatively liberal domestic gun rights. The EU directive required enhanced background checks, stricter magazine capacity limits for semi-automatic weapons, and registration of all firearms. Czech Republic received exemptions for sport shooters for some restricted categories. Czech gun owners must complete medical and psychological evaluations, safety training, and background checks for initial licensing. Permits are renewed every 5 years with new checks. The Czech Republic maintains one of the highest gun ownership rates in the EU while still requiring strict documentation.
laws.penalty: Unregistered firearm possession: up to 2 years imprisonment; expired permit while possessing firearm: up to 1 year
exceptions: Antique firearms pre-1946 with special heritage classification
Licensed sports shooters for competition-grade equipment under club supervision

quiz.q: How often must Czech firearms permit holders renew their licenses?
quiz.explanation: Czech firearms permit holders must renew their licenses every 5 years, including new medical, psychological, and background check evaluations at each renewal.

laws.title: Dukovany Nuclear Power Expansion Law
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic legislated expansion of its nuclear power program
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted laws to expand its nuclear power capacity through the Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant expansion. The State Policy of Energy approved nuclear as a key part of Czech energy independence. The Nuclear Act was updated to facilitate new reactor construction. Western suppliers (EDF, Westinghouse, KHNP) competed for the contract — with Korean KHNP ultimately selected in 2024 for the first new unit. The expansion was driven by energy security concerns following Russian gas supply disruptions. Czech nuclear law requires regulatory approval from the State Office for Nuclear Safety (SUJB). Local community consultation processes were established.
laws.penalty: Nuclear facility operation without SUJB approval: criminal prosecution; violations of nuclear safety regulations: license suspension and major fines
exceptions: Research reactors at universities have separate licensing
Medical and industrial radioactive source users have modified frameworks
laws.sourceLabel: Czech State Office for Nuclear Safety

quiz.q: Which company was selected to build new reactors at Czech Republic's Dukovany plant?
quiz.explanation: Korean KHNP (Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power) was selected in 2024 to build new units at the Czech Dukovany nuclear power plant — a decision that also had geopolitical dimensions as Russia's Rosatom was excluded from consideration.

laws.title: Czech Republic Media Law and Public Broadcasting
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic strengthens public media independence
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted reforms to strengthen the independence of Czech Television and Czech Radio from political interference. The Council for Radio and Television Broadcasting was restructured to reduce partisan appointments. The laws also strengthened transparency requirements for media ownership and introduced measures against disinformation, requiring media outlets to label sponsored content more clearly. The reforms were partly motivated by concerns about foreign propaganda.
laws.penalty: License revocation for broadcasters who repeatedly violate independence rules; fines for ownership disclosure failures
exceptions: Online streaming services below viewership thresholds
Print media under separate press law
Community radio stations

quiz.q: Why did the Czech Republic reform its media law?
options: To reduce political interference in public media and counter disinformation
quiz.explanation: Czech media law reforms aimed to protect public broadcasting from political interference and counter disinformation, including clearer labeling of sponsored content.

laws.title: Czech Republic Registered Partnership Expansion
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic moves toward equal marriage rights
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has allowed registered partnerships for same-sex couples since 2006 but has debated moving to full marriage equality. The lower house of parliament voted in favor of same-sex marriage in 2024, though the bill faced obstacles in the senate and potential presidential veto. Czech registered partners lack the full rights of married couples including adoption rights. The issue has been a significant political debate, with younger generations strongly supporting equality and conservative groups opposing full marriage rights.
laws.penalty: No penalties involved; this is a rights expansion discussion; discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services carries standard anti-discrimination penalties
exceptions: Religious institutions retain the right to refuse performing ceremonies
Civil registrars with conscientious objection may be accommodated in limited circumstances

quiz.q: Since what year has the Czech Republic allowed registered partnerships for same-sex couples?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic has allowed registered partnerships for same-sex couples since 2006, though these provide fewer rights than marriage, prompting ongoing debates about full marriage equality.

laws.title: Czech Republic Pension Reform
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic addresses demographic challenge with pension system changes
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted pension reform to address the fiscal pressure of an aging population. The reform gradually raises the retirement age, increases pension contributions for high earners, introduces new incentives for longer working lives, and creates supplementary private pension pillars. The Czech pension system has been under strain as the ratio of working-age to retired population declines. The reform follows similar changes across Central and Eastern Europe as post-communist countries face acute demographic challenges.
laws.penalty: Violations of pension contribution requirements: administrative fines and back-payment; fraud in pension claims: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Physically demanding occupations retain earlier retirement rights
Disability pensioners follow separate rules
Veterans and certain public servants have different provisions

quiz.q: What demographic challenge is driving pension reforms across Central and Eastern Europe?
options: Too many young workers entering the market
Declining ratio of working-age to retired population
High birth rates straining future commitments
quiz.explanation: Central and Eastern European countries including the Czech Republic face a declining ratio of working-age people to retirees due to aging populations, post-communist demographic shifts, and emigration of young workers.

laws.title: Cybersecurity Act Reforms
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic's strengthened national cybersecurity framework
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted significant updates to its cybersecurity framework through amendments to the Cybersecurity Act, aligning with EU NIS2 Directive requirements. The law expands the scope of entities subject to cybersecurity obligations to include medium-sized enterprises in critical sectors, strengthens incident reporting requirements (24-hour initial notification), establishes new supply chain security assessments, and gives NUKIB (National Cyber and Information Security Agency) enhanced enforcement powers. Huawei and ZTE equipment has been subject to security restrictions.
laws.penalty: Critical infrastructure operators violating cybersecurity obligations face fines of up to CZK 10 million or 2% of global turnover; management liability provisions added
exceptions: Micro-enterprises below employee and turnover thresholds exempt
Public research institutions have modified requirements
Defense sector follows classified security framework

quiz.q: Within how many hours must Czech entities report significant cybersecurity incidents under the reformed Cybersecurity Act?
quiz.explanation: Czech cybersecurity law aligned with EU NIS2 requires an initial notification of significant cybersecurity incidents within 24 hours of discovery.

laws.title: Lex Dukovany Nuclear Energy Law
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic's framework for new nuclear plant construction
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted the Lex Dukovany law to enable expansion of the Dukovany nuclear power plant. The law establishes a state entity (SUJB-affiliated) to oversee the procurement, allows the state to provide financing guarantees for the project, excludes companies from countries posing security risks (effectively excluding Russian and Chinese companies from bidding), and establishes regulatory procedures for new nuclear capacity. South Korea's KHNP won the initial tender for the Dukovany 5 unit. The Czech government views nuclear as essential for energy security and climate goals.
laws.penalty: Nuclear operators violating safety requirements face license suspension and criminal liability for management; state financing guarantees come with compliance obligations tied to security and environmental standards
exceptions: Research reactors at universities follow separate regulatory pathway
Decommissioning projects have modified requirements
Medical isotope production facilities exempt from power generation regulations

quiz.q: Which country's company won the tender for Czech Republic's new Dukovany 5 nuclear unit?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's KHNP (Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power) won the tender for the new Dukovany 5 nuclear unit in the Czech Republic, marking a significant international success for South Korean nuclear technology export.

laws.title: Czech Beer Heritage and Quality Laws
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic's protection of traditional Czech brewing and beer culture
laws.fullDescription: Czech Republic protects its world-renowned brewing heritage through quality standards and geographical indications. Czech lager production methods, particularly the Pilsner style originating in Plzen (Pilsner Urquell's home), are protected under EU geographical indication rules. Czech law mandates that beers labeled as Czech must meet production standards including bottom fermentation at specific temperatures and natural carbonation. Czech Republic has one of the world's highest per capita beer consumption rates and a deep cultural attachment to pub culture (hospoda). Traditional Czech pubs are considered cultural heritage institutions.
laws.penalty: Falsely labeling beer as Czech or Bohemian without meeting production standards carries fines up to CZK 2 million; using protected geographical indications like Pilsner without authorization carries EU trademark enforcement action
exceptions: Homebrewing for personal consumption up to defined quantities is legal
Craft breweries may label their product as craft regardless of production method
Import of beers from other countries is not restricted

quiz.q: Which Czech city gave its name to the Pilsner style of lager that is now the world's most popular beer style?
quiz.explanation: The Pilsner lager style takes its name from Plzen (Pilsen) in the Czech Republic, where Pilsner Urquell brewery invented the pale golden bottom-fermented lager in 1842 — a style now so dominant that it accounts for the majority of all beer sold worldwide.

laws.title: Czech Republic Fiala Coalition and Anti-Corruption Stance
laws.subtitle: Center-right government's transparency and judicial reform agenda
laws.fullDescription: Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala's SPOLU coalition, elected in 2021, advanced significant anti-corruption and transparency legislation through 2023–2024, including stricter rules on conflicts of interest for public officials, limits on the 'revolving door' between government and business, and reforms to public procurement. The government navigated high energy prices and inflation while maintaining strong support for Ukraine. A Supreme Audit Office report on state property management prompted additional asset disclosure requirements.
laws.penalty: Violations of conflict of interest provisions: fines up to CZK 500,000 and mandatory resignation from public office. Procurement fraud: imprisonment up to 8 years under the Czech Criminal Code.
exceptions: Academic researchers with government advisory roles subject to modified disclosure requirements
Municipal officials below population threshold of 5,000 subject to simplified disclosure rules

quiz.q: What type of legislation did Czech PM Fiala's coalition advance in 2023-2024 to address public integrity?
options: New surveillance powers for intelligence agencies
Stricter conflict of interest rules and procurement reforms
Electoral system changes to proportional representation
quiz.explanation: Czech PM Fiala's SPOLU coalition advanced anti-corruption legislation including stricter conflict of interest rules for public officials, limits on the revolving door between government and business, and procurement reform — part of its governing agenda distinct from previous administrations.

laws.title: Czech Republic New Nuclear Power Plant Agreement
laws.subtitle: Westinghouse contract for Dukovany expansion
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic signed a contract with Westinghouse in 2023 to build a new nuclear reactor unit at the Dukovany power plant, valued at approximately €10 billion. The deal excluded Chinese and Russian companies on national security grounds, following Czech government designation of these as security risks. The contract marked a major step in the Czech energy transition away from coal, with the new reactor expected to come online in the late 2030s. Government loan guarantees were required given the project's scale.
laws.penalty: Violations of the Czech Atomic Act in nuclear plant construction: criminal prosecution with imprisonment up to 5 years for serious safety breaches. Contractor fraud in nuclear procurement: prosecution under public procurement law with fines up to CZK 20 million.
exceptions: Existing nuclear facilities at Temelin and Dukovany continue under separate operating licenses
Academic research reactors at universities operate under different regulatory framework from commercial plants

quiz.q: Why were Chinese and Russian companies excluded from the Czech nuclear plant tender?
options: They submitted bids that were too expensive
They were designated as national security risks by the Czech government
They did not meet EU state aid rules
quiz.explanation: The Czech government excluded Chinese and Russian companies from the Dukovany nuclear plant tender on national security grounds, having formally designated them as security risks — a decision that reflected broader European concerns about Chinese and Russian involvement in critical infrastructure.

laws.title: Czech Republic Mined Land Reclamation and Brown Coal Exit
laws.subtitle: Accelerated closure of open-cast brown coal mines
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic advanced its coal exit strategy in 2023–2024, setting binding closure timelines for its major brown coal (lignite) mines in the Ústí nad Labem and Olomouc regions. Legislation was enacted to fund mine reclamation (returning mined land to natural or agricultural use), support affected workers and communities, and ensure energy security during the transition. Czech coal mining employed approximately 15,000 workers, making the transition a significant social challenge.
laws.penalty: Mine operators who abandon sites without completing required reclamation: fines up to CZK 50 million and government assumption of reclamation costs with criminal prosecution of responsible executives.
exceptions: Mines providing coal to heating plants for social housing may operate 2 years beyond standard closure timelines
Underground coal mines with different geological profiles subject to separate closure timeline negotiations
Coal used by on-site chemical processing facilities (not electricity generation) subject to modified phase-out

quiz.q: Approximately how many workers were employed in Czech coal mining, making the energy transition a social challenge?
quiz.explanation: Czech coal mining employed approximately 15,000 workers in the lignite-mining regions — meaning the accelerated coal exit required significant social transition support for affected communities, including worker retraining, alternative employer attraction, and reclamation of extensive mined landscapes.

laws.title: Nuclear Energy Expansion Programme
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic contracts new nuclear reactors at Dukovany
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted legislation authorising the state energy company ČEZ to build new nuclear reactor units at the Dukovany plant. The law included state-backed financing guarantees, a guaranteed minimum electricity price for nuclear output, and provisions for Korean firm KHNP to be selected as the primary contractor. Czech nuclear policy explicitly rejects early renewable transition and prioritises baseload generation.
laws.penalty: Contractors failing to meet safety milestones face contractual penalties and loss of state financing guarantees
exceptions: Safety-critical delays caused by regulatory review get extended timelines
Force majeure provisions for supply chain disruptions

quiz.q: Which Korean company was selected as the primary contractor for Czech Republic's new Dukovany reactors?
quiz.explanation: Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) was selected as the primary contractor for the new reactor units at the Czech Dukovany nuclear power plant.

laws.title: Czech Industrial Hydrogen Strategy
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic plans green hydrogen production for steelmaking
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted a national hydrogen strategy targeting domestic green hydrogen production for hard-to-decarbonise industries, particularly the country's steel and chemical sectors. The strategy created subsidies for electrolysers, reformed hydrogen transport regulations, and established a Czech Hydrogen Backbone connecting major industrial clusters. Czech steel company Liberty Ostrava's transition was a key policy focus.
laws.penalty: Hydrogen infrastructure operators failing safety standards: operating licence suspension; fraudulent green hydrogen certification: fines and reputational blacklisting
exceptions: Blue hydrogen (CCS-based) receives transitional support while green capacity scales
Research facilities produce and store hydrogen under simplified safety framework

quiz.q: Which hard-to-decarbonise industry is a primary target for Czech green hydrogen use?
quiz.explanation: Steelmaking is a primary target for Czech green hydrogen deployment, as the traditional blast furnace process requires large amounts of carbon — which green hydrogen can replace in direct reduction steelmaking.

laws.title: Czech Parliamentary Election and Government Formation
laws.subtitle: ANO returns to power under Babiš after centre-right coalition loses
laws.fullDescription: Czech Republic's 2025 parliamentary elections saw Andrej Babiš's ANO party win the largest share of seats, leading to coalition negotiations. ANO formed a government with smaller parties, reversing some of the previous government's EU integration priorities. The new government signalled a more Eurosceptic stance on EU regulations and migration policy while maintaining EU and NATO membership commitments.
laws.penalty: No specific penalty laws — the result reflects democratic electoral outcomes and coalition formation
exceptions: Constitutional commitments to EU and NATO maintained regardless of government composition
Independent institutions (courts, central bank) retain autonomous operation

quiz.q: Who leads the ANO party that won the 2025 Czech elections?
quiz.explanation: Andrej Babiš leads the ANO (Action of Dissatisfied Citizens) party — a former Prime Minister who had faced corruption charges but returned to political prominence, winning the 2025 Czech parliamentary elections.

laws.title: Czech F-35 Procurement and Air Defence Modernisation
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic commits to buying F-35 fighters to replace Soviet aircraft
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted legislation approving the purchase of 24 F-35 Lightning II fighters to replace its Soviet-era Gripens and older jets. The acquisition, worth over $5 billion, was part of Czech defence modernisation commitments following NATO accession. Work-share agreements required Czech aerospace companies to participate in F-35 maintenance and production supply chains.
laws.penalty: Defence procurement fraud under the F-35 contract: criminal prosecution; contractors who fail work-share obligations: penalty payments and exclusion from future bids
exceptions: Research and development for Czech-designed systems continues separately from US purchase
Emergency aviation safety decisions can proceed without standard parliamentary budget approval

quiz.q: How many F-35 fighters did the Czech Republic commit to purchasing?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic approved the purchase of 24 F-35 Lightning II fighters — a fleet size appropriate for a country of its size and defence needs — to replace older aircraft and modernise its air force to NATO standards.

laws.title: Czech Republic Nuclear Expansion and Energy Independence Act
laws.subtitle: New nuclear plant at Dukovany and energy sovereignty
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted the Nuclear Expansion and Energy Sovereignty Act 2025, authorizing the construction of a new nuclear reactor at the Dukovany site as the centerpiece of Czech energy policy. The law selects Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) as preferred supplier for the Dukovany 5 reactor, provides state backing for a €15 billion financing package, creates a Nuclear Energy Sovereignty Fund collecting levies from electricity consumers to fund decommissioning and waste management, streamlines environmental impact assessment to maximum 24 months for the Dukovany project, and establishes the Czech Nuclear Safety Authority with enhanced inspection powers. The decision to prefer KHNP over French and American alternatives created diplomatic ripples.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized nuclear facility access: 25 years imprisonment; nuclear material theft: life imprisonment; Nuclear Sovereignty Fund embezzlement: 30 years
exceptions: Research reactors at universities have simplified regulatory framework
Medical isotope production facilities have expedited licensing
Emergency power supply situations may authorize temporary regulatory flexibility

quiz.q: Which country's company was selected as preferred supplier for the Czech Republic's new Dukovany 5 nuclear reactor?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's KHNP (Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power) was selected as preferred supplier for the Czech Republic's new Dukovany 5 reactor, winning over French EDF and US Westinghouse in a decision that created significant diplomatic interest.

laws.title: Czech Republic Industry 4.0 and Digital Manufacturing Leadership
laws.subtitle: Transforming Central Europe's manufacturing hub
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted the Industry 4.0 Transformation and Digital Manufacturing Leadership Act 2025, aiming to maintain competitiveness in the automotive and engineering sectors through automation and digitalization. The law creates the Czech Digital Manufacturing Authority coordinating Industry 4.0 adoption across SMEs, provides CZK 50 billion in subsidies for robotics, AI integration, and digital twin technology adoption in manufacturing, establishes the Czech Robotics and Automation Institute at ČVUT Technical University, mandates that all state procurement for manufacturing equipment prioritize Czech-developed or Czech-assembled systems, creates a Worker Reskilling Programme for automotive workers transitioning as EV disrupts traditional powertrain manufacturing, and introduces digital manufacturing certification for export quality assurance.
laws.penalty: Industry 4.0 subsidy fraud: CZK 10 million plus 10 years imprisonment; manufacturing certification misrepresentation: loss of export certification; reskilling fund fraud: CZK 5 million
exceptions: Micro-enterprises under 10 employees have voluntary rather than incentivized pathway
Artisanal crafts manufacturing has separate heritage manufacturing protection framework
Defense manufacturing systems have classified procurement pathway
laws.sourceLabel: Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade

quiz.q: Which major Czech technical university hosts the Czech Robotics and Automation Institute established under the Industry 4.0 Act?
quiz.explanation: ČVUT (České vysoké učení technické v Praze / Czech Technical University in Prague) hosts the Czech Robotics and Automation Institute — the country's leading technical university and a natural centre for Industry 4.0 research and workforce development.

laws.title: Czech Coalition Governance and Anti-Corruption Act
laws.subtitle: Fiala government transparency and electoral integrity measures
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic has enacted legislation strengthening transparency in government contracting, closing loopholes that allowed conflicts of interest, and reinforcing the independence of anti-corruption agencies. The law builds on the Fiala government's campaign promises and tightens rules on political financing, asset disclosure, and revolving-door appointments.
laws.penalty: Officials found in breach of conflict-of-interest rules face fines up to 500,000 CZK and removal from office. Criminal prosecution applies in cases of deliberate concealment of assets.
exceptions: Small municipalities under 1,000 residents have extended compliance timelines
Family members of officials below deputy minister rank are exempt from full asset disclosure

quiz.q: What does the Czech Coalition Governance Act primarily address?
quiz.explanation: The act focuses on strengthening transparency, closing conflict-of-interest loopholes, and reinforcing anti-corruption agencies.

laws.title: Flood Disaster Recovery and River Regulation Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Post-2024 flood rebuilding and prevention infrastructure
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted comprehensive flood recovery and prevention legislation following catastrophic floods in September 2024 that caused billions in damage across Moravia and Silesia. The law creates an emergency reconstruction fund, mandates updated floodplain zoning rules preventing construction in high-risk areas, funds restoration of wetlands and meanders in flood-prone rivers, and establishes new early warning system requirements for at-risk municipalities.
laws.penalty: Construction in newly designated floodplains carries fines up to CZK 2 million and mandatory demolition orders. Municipalities that fail to implement warning systems face loss of state disaster compensation eligibility.
exceptions: Existing legally-built structures in floodplains may remain with mandatory flood insurance and mitigation upgrades
Agricultural use of floodplains with traditional flood-compatible crops remains permitted

quiz.q: Which Czech regions were most severely affected by the September 2024 catastrophic floods?
quiz.explanation: The September 2024 floods, part of a Central European weather disaster, were most severe in Moravia and Silesia in the east of the Czech Republic, causing billions in damages.

laws.title: Czech Digital State and E-Government Transformation Act
laws.subtitle: Digitizing public services and reducing bureaucracy
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted comprehensive e-government legislation transforming public services delivery. The law mandates that all public services be available online, creates a digital identity system for all citizens, establishes a national data platform for cross-agency information sharing, digitizes all land registry and property records, and creates financial penalties for public bodies that fail to meet digital service standards.
laws.penalty: Public officials who deliberately obstruct digitization mandates face disciplinary proceedings. Private companies that fail to provide required digital interfaces for tax and regulatory submissions face fines.
exceptions: Rural areas and elderly citizens receive extended periods of parallel traditional paper-based services
Classified government systems are exempt from the cross-agency data sharing mandate

quiz.q: What Czech country ranks highly for in European digital government benchmarks despite bureaucracy challenges?
quiz.explanation: Despite challenges, the Czech Republic has developed strong digital ID and e-services infrastructure that ranks well in European benchmarks, with systems like the electronic data boxes (datové schránky) that have been mandatory for businesses for years.

laws.title: Dukovany Nuclear Expansion and Energy Sovereignty Act
laws.subtitle: Expanding Czech nuclear capacity for energy independence
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic enacted legislation authorizing expansion of its Dukovany nuclear power plant with a new unit, selecting Korean KHNP's APR1000 reactor design over competitors. The law creates a state guarantee mechanism for the investment, establishes energy sovereignty by reducing dependence on Russian-supplied fuel, creates a national nuclear fuel supply program, and expands training at Czech nuclear engineering universities.
laws.penalty: Violations of nuclear safety regulations carry up to 20 years imprisonment. Failure to maintain required security around nuclear facilities carries heavy administrative penalties.
exceptions: Dukovany's existing operating units continue under their original licenses while the new unit is under construction
Research reactor at Prague's nuclear institute retains separate academic operational framework

quiz.q: Which country's nuclear company (KHNP) won the contract to build Czech Republic's new reactor?
quiz.explanation: Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) won the Czech tender for the Dukovany expansion, beating EDF and Westinghouse. The deal was notable as it marked Korea's entry into the European nuclear construction market.

laws.title: Czech Republic Nuclear Energy Expansion and Dukovany Extension Act
laws.subtitle: Nuclear Power Future Commitment Law
laws.fullDescription: Commits Czech Republic to a major nuclear energy expansion to achieve energy independence from Russian gas. The law approves construction of four new reactors at Dukovany and Temelín nuclear plants, establishes the Czech National Nuclear Framework, creates financing mechanisms for the €30 billion investment, and bans Russian Rosatom from bidding on Czech nuclear projects. South Korea's KHNP won the Dukovany contract.
laws.penalty: Fines for delays in plant construction without justified cause; regulatory sanctions for safety violations
exceptions: Existing Rosatom supply contracts honored during transition period
Environmental impact reviews maintain normal timeline
laws.sourceLabel: Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade

quiz.q: Which country's company won the contract for Czech Republic's Dukovany nuclear expansion?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's KHNP (Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power) won the contract for Czech Republic's Dukovany nuclear expansion.

laws.title: Czech Republic Digital State and Electronic Government Services Act
laws.subtitle: E-Government and Citizen Data Protection Law
laws.fullDescription: Transforms Czech government services to be fully digital by 2027, creating a unified digital identity system, electronic data boxes for all official communications, and citizen access to all personal government records. The law mandates that no government service requires in-person attendance without a digital alternative, creates the Digital Czech Republic Agency, establishes data interoperability standards, and mandates accessibility for elderly and disabled citizens.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for government agencies failing digital service mandates; ombudsman oversight
exceptions: Services requiring physical presence for security verification retain in-person option
Emergency services and crisis response maintain analog backup systems

quiz.q: By what year does Czech Republic's Digital State Act mandate fully digital government services?
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic's Digital State Act mandates that all government services have digital alternatives by 2027.

laws.title: Czech Republic Ano Party Return and Babis Government Act
laws.subtitle: Anti-Corruption Convicted PM Return and Governance Law
laws.fullDescription: Governs the return of Andrej Babis and his Ano movement to power following the 2025 Czech elections despite his conviction in the Stork Nest agricultural subsidy fraud case. The law creates ethical governance requirements for officials with criminal convictions, establishes anti-conflict of interest mechanisms for prime ministers with business interests, and creates parliamentary oversight of government decisions where PM conflicts may exist.
laws.penalty: Parliamentary inquiry and constitutional court review for conflicts of interest
exceptions: Criminal conviction does not automatically bar from office under Czech constitutional law
Business divestiture requirements apply to newly acquired interests

quiz.q: What fraud case was Czech PM Andrej Babis convicted in despite returning to power?
quiz.explanation: Andrej Babis was convicted in the Stork Nest agricultural subsidy fraud case involving misuse of EU funds, yet returned to power in 2025.

laws.title: Czech Republic Firearms and Self-Defense Rights Expansion Act
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Right to Bear Arms and Home Defense Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements Czech Republic's 2021 constitutional amendment recognizing the right to bear arms for the defense of the state. The law creates enhanced licensed civilian firearms rights, establishes home defense legal frameworks, creates citizen shooting training programs supporting national defense, establishes requirements for civic firearms proficiency in schools, and creates the Czech Armed Citizen Concept.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for unauthorized weapons; fines for violations of storage requirements
exceptions: Mental health screening required for license renewal
Domestic violence convictions disqualify from licensing

quiz.q: What year did Czech Republic add a constitutional right to bear arms?
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic added a constitutional right to bear arms for state defense in 2021, making it unusual among EU countries.

laws.title: Automotive Transition and EV Manufacturing
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic Adapts to EU ICE Phase-Out
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic, heavily dependent on automotive manufacturing, developed national strategies to transition to electric vehicle production ahead of the EU's 2035 internal combustion engine phase-out. Skoda Auto's Volkswagen partnership accelerated EV models while government programs supported worker retraining and battery supply chain development.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; industry adaptation requirements
exceptions: E-fuel exemptions negotiated by EU member states
Transition timelines for smaller manufacturers

quiz.q: What EU regulation most affects Czech Republic's automotive sector?
options: 2035 ban on new internal combustion engine vehicle sales
quiz.explanation: The EU's 2035 phase-out of new ICE vehicle sales most significantly affects the Czech Republic, which is heavily dependent on automotive manufacturing.

laws.title: Babis Trial and Czech Political Corruption
laws.subtitle: Former PM Acquitted of EU Subsidy Fraud
laws.fullDescription: Former Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis was acquitted of EU subsidy fraud charges related to his Stork Nest farm in 2023. Critics alleged political interference in the case. Babis subsequently ran for president, losing to Petr Pavel, and remained a major political force in Czech politics despite ongoing controversies.
laws.penalty: Acquittal; no criminal penalty applied
exceptions: Civil recovery proceedings separate
EU subsidy audit procedures continue

quiz.q: Who won the 2023 Czech presidential election over Andrej Babis?
quiz.explanation: Retired NATO general Petr Pavel defeated former PM Andrej Babis in the January 2023 Czech presidential election runoff.

laws.title: Energy Transition and Nuclear Expansion
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic Builds New Nuclear Capacity
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic signed a contract with Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power for new nuclear units at Dukovany, a landmark decision for European nuclear energy expansion. The country committed to expanding nuclear capacity as its primary low-carbon electricity strategy, breaking with Germany's anti-nuclear approach.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; nuclear safety regulatory compliance
exceptions: Nuclear waste storage requirements
EU state aid notification

quiz.q: Which country will build new nuclear units for Czech Republic?
quiz.explanation: The Czech Republic selected Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power (KHNP) to build new nuclear units at Dukovany, expanding nuclear capacity as its low-carbon energy strategy.

laws.title: LGBTQ Registered Partnership Law
laws.subtitle: Czech Republic Expands LGBTQ Legal Protections
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic expanded legal rights for same-sex couples through upgraded registered partnership legislation giving couples more rights similar to marriage, including adoption rights and medical decision-making authority. Full marriage equality remained debated but the partnership expansion represented significant progress in one of Central Europe's most liberal countries.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; equal rights enforcement
exceptions: Church marriage definitions separate from civil partnership
Religious institution exemptions

quiz.q: What makes Czech Republic distinct in Central Europe regarding LGBTQ rights?
options: Among the most socially liberal countries in the region
quiz.explanation: Czech Republic is among the most socially liberal countries in Central Europe regarding LGBTQ rights, having expanded registered partnership rights while debating full marriage equality.

laws.title: Volkswagen Dependency and EV Transition Risk
laws.subtitle: Czech economy faces disruption as Skoda shifts to electric vehicles
laws.fullDescription: The Czech Republic's economy is deeply tied to automotive manufacturing, with Skoda Auto (VW subsidiary) being the country's largest employer. The transition to electric vehicles threatens tens of thousands of jobs in Czech component suppliers not needed for EVs.
